transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10
Start: 15:00 UTC (08:00 PT)
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Patel (Acme Head of AI), Samir Rao (Acme Platform), Elena Gomes (Acme DS)

Summary (auto):
Quick alignment on success criteria for Acme's POC focused on clinical note summarization and structured extraction. Agreed deliverables: golden prompt set, automated eval harness, 2-week benchmark on Dedicated trial capacity, and security docs. Discussed scoring approach, hallucination checks, and format compliance thresholds.

Topics:
- Success criteria and acceptance thresholds
- Workload sizing and trial capacity
- Quality eval plan (golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination/format checks)
- Scoring approach and human-in-loop review
- Timelines and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone good morning, thanks for joining, quick roll call?
[00:07] Priya: Hi Priya here, sorry just coming in, running a bit late's my calendar was messy.
[00:11] Samir: Samir on the line.
[00:13] Elena: Elena here.
[00:15] Maya: Maya from Redwood. Jordan as well.
[00:19] Jordan: Cool thanks. The idea for today is to scope the quality eval plan for the POC - specifically for the clinical note summarization and structured extraction use cases. We'll go through success criteria, dataset size, benchmarks, and the actual eval metrics and golden prompts.
[00:34] Priya: Sounds good. For context, our main goal is to replace a manual coding step for inpatient discharge summaries and extract problem list, meds, and action items. Accuracy and hallucination control are both critical, also format compliance - payloads go into downstream ETL.
[00:48] Jordan: Understood. Can you remind us of the traffic and typical lengths?
[00:52] Samir: Most notes are 400-1,200 tokens, average around 650. Expected peak throughput for the pilot maybe 5 qps, steady 1-2 qps. We can batch on our side but want low tail latency for interactive review.
[01:08] Maya: Great. For sizing we recommended a two-week Dedicated trial with 1 GPU pool and autoscale headroom to simulate diurnal peaks. That should cover the benchmark. We'll capture p50/p95 token latencies and throughput.
[01:22] Elena: For quality, what thresholds should we aim for? Our internal bar is fairly high — we want extraction F1 > 0.88 for problem list and meds, and hallucination under 3% on blinded review.
[01:36] Jordan: That sounds reasonable as a starting point. On Redwood side we propose acceptance criteria for the POC:
- Extraction F1 >= 0.85 on the golden test set
- Structured format compliance >= 95% (JSON schema validated)
- Hallucination rate <= 2% measured by random audit + automated hallucination heuristics
- P95 token latency under 450ms for 512 token prompt + 128 token response under Dedicated trial

[02:05] Priya: The 2% hallucination threshold seems aggressive but acceptable for POC if we pair with human review. We'll also want regression tests to make sure model updates don't degrade format or hallucination.
[02:19] Maya: Agreed. So the quality eval plan we discussed: golden prompts, regression suite, hallucination detectors, format/schema checks, automated scoring plus sampling for human review. We'll break those down.

[02:30] Jordan: Golden prompt set - we'll provide ~200 gold prompts covering the most common note variants: discharge summary, progress note, consult note, and tricky edge cases (merged notes, clinician shorthand). These will include expected structured extraction outputs. We'll keep some reserved as holdout for final evaluation (e.g., 50 examples).
[02:50] Elena: Can the gold prompts include redaction markers? We will de-identify but keep clinical markers like [MED] or [PROB] for the eval.
[02:58] Jordan: Yes, please include de-identified placeholders.

[03:02] Maya: Regression tests - approach is to store golden prompts + expected outputs, run them through each candidate model and diff the structured outputs. The regression suite will flag: missing fields, schema violations, token mismatches, and major semantic shifts. We also keep a historical baseline to detect quality drift.
[03:24] Samir: For regression we need deterministic runs. How do you handle nondeterminism with sampling-based decoding?
[03:30] Jordan: We'll run deterministic top-k for the eval or set a fixed random seed and use top-p with a seed. For extraction tasks we prefer deterministic decoding (greedy or beam with small beam) to ensure comparability. We'll note in the harness config.
[03:47] Priya: Hallucination detection — what heuristics do you use?
[03:50] Maya: A combination: 1) entity-level cross-checks against input (e.g., meds mentioned in source), 2) factuality classifiers trained to detect unsupported assertions, 3) regex/semantic checks for impossible values (e.g., DOB in future), and 4) human sampling. We'll run automated detectors as first pass and then sample 500 outputs for human audit to estimate real hallucination rate with confidence intervals.
[04:14] Jordan: We'll also include a metadata flag for uncertain answers so downstream UI can prompt reviewer.
[04:20] Elena: Scoring approach — what metrics will you compute?
[04:24] Jordan: For structured extraction: precision, recall, F1 at entity level (exact match + partial match variants). For summarization/notes we'll compute ROUGE-L and BERTScore as a sanity check but primary is task-specific F1. For format: schema validation pass rate. For hallucination: percent of outputs flagged by detectors and percent of audited samples with unsupported content.
[04:46] Priya: Can you provide the exact scoring script? We need to plug the outputs into our QA pipeline.
[04:51] Maya: Yes, we'll share an eval harness on GitHub (or private repo) with a Docker runner and a single command: run_eval.sh --gold gold.json --pred preds.json --schema schema.json. We'll make the scoring outputs in CSV with per-example metrics and an aggregate summary.
[05:08] Samir: For performance benchmarks we want p50/p95/p99 token latency and tokens-per-second. Also cost estimate per 1M tokens for each model variant.
[05:19] Jordan: We'll provide cost-per-token estimates for the tested model variants and run load tests to produce TPS curves. We can also report cost per processed note at median and peak.
[05:30] Priya: Timeline for the POC?
[05:33] Jordan: Proposed timeline: 1) This week - exchange golden prompts and sample dataset (by 2025-09-12). 2) Next week - Redwood sets up Dedicated trial and runs initial benchmark (start 2025-09-15). 3) Week after - run full eval and human audit (finish by 2025-09-26). 4) Final review and decision meeting by 2025-09-29.
[05:52] Priya: That works for us. Any security blockers?
[05:55] Maya: We need to ensure KMS integration and VPC peering for Dedicated trial. We'll provide our Private deployment security pack (SOC2, ISO docs, audit log flow).
[06:07] Samir: We have an internal compliance check for KMS in our VPC — I need to confirm our key policies but peering should be fine. There might be a firewall rule we need to add.
[06:17] Jordan: We'll include network checklist in the next email.
[06:20] Elena: Back to evaluation specifics — what about regression/rollouts? If you update model mid-POC how do we compare?
[06:27] Maya: We'll snapshot model versions and run the same golden set on each version. Redwood's rollout can do canary vs baseline and we'll produce a diff report highlighting regressions by metric and by prompt. We'll also attach the raw outputs for manual triage.
[06:43] Priya: For hallucination definition, we'll provide a few negative examples that count as critical failure (e.g., inventing a medication not in record). These should be zero tolerance.
[06:54] Jordan: Put those in the golden set as 'critical failures' — the harness will mark any instance as FAIL and escalate.
[07:00] Samir: For the human audit sample size, what's realistic to get +/-2% margin?
[07:05] Maya: For a 95% confidence interval with margin +/-2% and expected ~3% hallucination, you'd need about 500-600 samples. We recommended 500 for POC.
[07:18] Elena: And what about format enforcement? We need strict JSON schema. If model returns free text, auto-reject.
[07:24] Jordan: We'll run a two-stage check: 1) syntactic JSON parse check, 2) schema validation (types, required fields). If parse fails, auto-fail and count as a schema violation. We'll provide schema in the repo.
[07:38] Priya: Can we automate remediation like asking the model for "fix the JSON" and do a second pass?
[07:44] Maya: Yes, that's a common pattern — "auto-fix" pass with a specialized prompt and then re-validate. But for acceptance metrics we treat the first response as primary, and auto-fix counts as a secondary metric (we'll report both).
[08:00] Jordan: Benchmarks - we'll run on three model variants: 1) baseline open model (v1), 2) Redwood-curated quantized variant (v1-q), 3) fallback smaller model for cost tradeoffs. We'll report quality vs cost curves.
[08:17] Samir: For the Dedicated trial can we pin a model version?
[08:19] Maya: Yes you can pin a model version for the run; we'll also demonstrate automated fallback policies but for apples-to-apples we pin during the benchmark.
[08:26] Priya: For evaluation rubric — can you show an example scoring breakdown per example?
[08:29] Jordan: Example CSV row: example_id, gold_entities, pred_entities, precision, recall, f1, schema_pass(yes/no), halluc_flag(yes/no), notes. Aggregate: mean F1, schema_pass_rate, hallucination_rate. We'll also surface per-entity class F1 (meds, problems, actions).
[08:47] Elena: What about partial matches e.g., 'lisinopril 10 mg' vs 'lisinopril' — how is that scored?
[08:52] Maya: We support token-level overlap and normalized entity matching that strips dosing modifiers for primary entity match and compute both exact and partial scores. We'll report both.
[09:02] Priya: One operational ask: include a small web UI or CSV that our reviewers can use to quickly mark hallucinations and reason codes.
[09:09] Jordan: We'll provide a simple review UI for the audit sample with ability to tag reason codes (invented_entity, incorrect_value, missing_context). Export CSV for your QA pipeline.
[09:20] Samir: Are you able to run privacy-preserving evals if we can't share real PHI?
[09:25] Maya: Yes - we support de-identified placeholders and synthetically augmented examples. We can also run the eval in your VPC/Private deployment if needed.
[09:34] Priya: Great. Any known edge cases we should be aware of?
[09:37] Jordan: Things like merged note sections, multiple clinicians' notes in a single document, heavy shorthand/abbrev. We'll include edge-case prompts in the golden set and document failure modes in the report.
[09:51] Elena: For results presentation, show both raw metrics and example failures with context. That's what leadership asks for.
[09:58] Jordan: We'll include a 'top 20 failure cases' appendix in the report.
[10:02] Priya: On data residency - are logs or token traces stored off-site during the trial?
[10:08] Maya: For Dedicated trial we can configure logs retention and KMS. We'll provide options so nothing leaves your VPC unless explicit.
[10:15] Samir: Ok I'll coordinate with our security team on KMS policies.
[10:18] Jordan: Good. Quick recap and next steps?
[10:22] Jordan: Action items: Jordan send golden prompts and eval harness; Maya set up trial; Priya send sample de-id dataset; Samir confirm network. We've captured due dates.
[10:34] Priya: Fine with that, we'll review once we get the harness.
[10:37] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark run and the decision review.
[10:42] Maya: Thanks all.
[10:45] (call ends)

Notes on scoring thresholds (from call, paraphrased):
- Extraction F1 >= 0.85 is POC pass, 0.88+ preferred
- Schema compliance >= 95%
- Hallucination <= 2% target, up to 3% acceptable with human review
- Latency: p95 <= 450ms for typical prompt length (512 in, 128 out)

References & artifacts mentioned:
- Eval harness repo (will be shared): run_eval.sh, gold.json, schema.json, scoring.csv
- Security pack link: redwood.com/security/soc2 (placeholder)
- Benchmark spreadsheet: costs_vs_quality.xlsx (shared after call)

End of transcript.
